head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: (earliest, latest) round in which players at positions f < s meet, with n players left
They are opposite each other, so they play in this round → (1, 1)
Mirror the row: the same game with positions (n+1−s, n+1−f)
Reduces the problem to the left-leaning case
Players left in the next round
a in range(f), b in range(s − f)
a players before f and b players between f and s may advance (any count is allowed because the other results can be chosen freely)
Enumerating every possible outcome of the other matches
Next round positions of the two stars
When s is in the first half
s lies in the right half; players between the opponent of s and s pair among themselves, adding (s − o)//2 more winners before s
Add this round to the earliest/latest from the next state

p: `n = 11`, `firstPlayer = 2`, `secondPlayer = 4`. They do not meet this round (2 + 4 = 6 < 12). The next round has 6 players; the four possible new position pairs and their results are:
The smallest first value is 2 and the largest second value is 3. Adding the current round gives `[3, 4]`.

bullets: Time: about O(n⁴) states-times-choices in the worst case, small for n ≤ 28.

1900.takeaway: Memoised search on (players left, position of each star): enumerate how many other players advance before and between them, and combine the outcomes.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Concatenate the numbers as text, e.g. 9 9 9 9 → "9999"
Sum of the digits, turned back into text for the next round

p: `leetcode`, `k = 2`: the string becomes `12552031545`; round 1 gives `1+2+5+5+2+0+3+1+5+4+5 = 33`; round 2 gives `3+3 = 6`.

bullets: Time: O(n) for the conversion; later rounds shrink quickly.

1945.takeaway: Build the digit string once, then replace it by its digit sum k times.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Sum of absolute values, the best possible if every sign could be positive
Smallest absolute value in the matrix
Flipping two adjacent cells changes the number of negatives by 0 or ±2, so its parity stays
If the parity is odd, one value must stay negative; choose the smallest

p: `matrix = [[1,-1],[-1,1]]`: absolute values sum to 4, there are 2 negatives (even).
`[[1,2,3],[-1,-2,-3],[1,2,3]]`: total = 18, 3 negatives (odd), smallest absolute value 1, so the answer is `18 − 2 = 16`.

1975.takeaway: The number of negatives keeps its parity; if it is odd, sacrifice the element with the smallest absolute value.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: OR of the whole array, which is the largest OR any subset can reach
Decide for element i: include or exclude, with the OR so far in cur
All elements decided: count 1 if cur equals target

p: Two subsets reach the maximum OR, so the answer is 2. The empty subset gives 0, which differs from the target because all numbers are positive.

2044.takeaway: The maximum OR is the OR of everything; try all 2ⁿ subsets and count those that reach it.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A sliding window of three neighbouring nodes
Smallest gap between neighbouring critical points
Largest gap, between the first and last

p: Gaps between neighbours: 2 and 1, so the minimum is 1. The largest distance is `5 − 2 = 3`. The answer is `[1, 3]`.

bullets: Space: O(n) for the position list.

2058.takeaway: Record the positions of local extremes in one pass; the minimum distance is between neighbours and the maximum is last minus first.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Required size of the current group (1, 2, 3, ...)
Collects up to `size` nodes of this group
Reverse only groups with even length (the last group may be shorter)
Reverses by rewriting the values instead of the links
Continues after the group with the next size

p: `[5,6,2,3,9,1,4,8,3,7]`. A final group shorter than its turn is reversed only if its actual length is even.

bullets: Space: O(√n) for one group at a time (group sizes grow by one).

2074.takeaway: Walk the list in groups of size 1, 2, 3, ...; for every group of even actual length, reverse its values.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Sum of subarray maxima when less is true, subarray minima when false
Indices whose values are in monotone order; popping finds the nearest bigger (or smaller) neighbour
The element whose span is now known
Nearest earlier element that is not smaller (or bigger)
nums[mid] is the max/min of (mid − left) × (i − mid) subarrays
Sum of maxima minus sum of minima = sum of ranges

p: `nums = [1,2,3]`. Contribution of each element as the maximum:
Sum of maxima = 14. As the minimum: 3 contributes `3×1×1 = 3`, 2 contributes `2×1×2 = 4`, 1 contributes `1×1×3 = 3`, so the sum of minima = 10. Answer: `14 − 10 = 4`.
In ties the boundary rules (strict on one side, non-strict on the other) make every subarray count exactly once.

2104.takeaway: Sum of ranges = sum of maxima − sum of minima, and each of those is computed in O(n) with a monotonic stack.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: How many employees favour each person
Nobody likes them, so they are chain starts; peel them off
Longest chain of employees that leads into v
The cycles of the favourite graph
The cycle alone fills a table; chains cannot be attached
A pair can seat its two longest chains on each side: depth[a] + depth[b]; chains of different pairs can be combined

2127.takeaway: Each employee points to one favourite: peel off the chains, then the answer is either the longest cycle of length ≥ 3 or the sum of all 2-cycles with their longest chains.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Every section needs exactly 2 seats, so the count must be even and positive → 0 ways otherwise
Number of positions where the divider between pair (i−2, i−1) and pair (i, i+1) can go: after seat i−1 up to just before seat i
One gap between each pair of consecutive seat pairs

p: The divider between the first pair (seats at 0 and 1) and the second pair (4 and 6) can go after position 1, 2 or 3, so there are 3 ways.

2147.takeaway: Group the seats in pairs; between neighbouring pairs the divider can go in (distance) places, and the answer is the product of those distances.
